webTitle: Ohio Republican Max Miller faces growing calls to resign over domestic abuse allegations

fields.headline: Ohio Republican Max Miller faces growing calls to resign over domestic abuse allegations
fields.trailText: Miller calls women accusing him liars as Republican senator Bernie Moreno says former son-in-law unfit for Congress
fields.bodyText: Max Miller, the beleaguered US Republican representative from Ohio, has vowed to defy a rising groundswell of resignation calls from his own party over domestic abuse allegations after his ex-father-in-law, Bernie Moreno, a GOP senator, said he was unfit to serve in Congress. In a combative interview with CNN’s Jake Tapper, Miller turned the tables by attacking Moreno, accused three women – including his ex-wife – of lying by saying he had been violent towards them, and invoked Donald Trump in insisting that he would not resign. As a deadline loomed for party leaders to choose a potential replacement, Miller, a former White House aide, took an unapologetic stand a day after Trump himself brought pressure to bear by calling him and reportedly telling him “things aren’t looking good” for his re-election campaign against his Democratic opponent, Brian Poindexter. The congressional ethics committee launched an investigation into allegations that Miller “may have engaged in domestic violence and abuse or illegal drug use in violation of the code of official conduct or any other applicable standard of conduct”, it said on Tuesday. Earlier in the day, Miller said he would request an ethics investigation into himself “to clear my name from these horrific attacks on myself and family”, adding: “I have absolutely nothing to hide.” Pleas for Miller to step down intensified after Moreno – the father of Miller’s former wife, Emily Moreno – broke his silence after months of refraining from comment on allegations concerning the alleged abuse of his daughter. “If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them,” Moreno, an ally of Trump, posted on Sunday. “He should not serve in the House of Representatives.” Addressing reporters on Tuesday, Moreno described the dispute between his daughter and Miller as “truly the seventh level of hell”, adding: “This has been a horrific experience for my entire family. “This has been brutal beyond comprehension, and if there’s any minimum standard for being an elected official, as I said, he fails to meet that minimum basic standard.” Moreno said he had to handle the pickup of his granddaughter at a police station this weekend because he didn’t “want my daughter interacting with this man”. “I don’t know what this guy’s capable of,” he said. Moreno’s comments came after Miller posted a livestream video defending himself against the abuse accusations and saying his former wife had “significant mental-health challenges”. The senator also accused Miller of withholding a blue bunny from his small daughter that he said helped the toddler go to sleep – an allegation that drew a belligerent response from Miller when Tapper asked on The Lead if he had been guilty of “emotionally abusive behavior”. “I would agree that if that were true, that would be incredibly disturbing, and that the senator would be right,” Miller said. “However, he has taken two years to publicly acknowledge for me to resign from my seat. Why is that?” After a prolonged back-and-forth, Miller gave an unambiguous response when asked if Emily Moreno and two other women – including Stephanie Grisham, a former White House spokesperson in Trump’s first presidency – had lied in accusing him of treating them violently. “Yes, it’s very easy … Every single time, and people have asked me, what are you going to do? Are you going to drop out of this race? Are you going to resign? Are you going to get out before the deadline? And my answer to you, Jake, is no, and I can tell you why. “In 2016, when President Donald J Trump faced the most extreme allegations in the world that hit him day after day after day, and people in the media, very much like yourself and others, said that he would have no shot at winning, that he should not be the president of the United States. But guess what? He stayed in, and he was resilient. “So for no second am I going to sit here and continue to be debased by false and baseless allegations, and be pushed out of the seat I have worked so hard to represent and done a terrific job for our community.” Yet a series of public statements from Moreno’s fellow Republican senators indicate that their sympathies are with him. “[Miller] should resign. He should quit,” Roger Marshall, a senator from Kansas, told Politico. “I don’t know Mr Miller’s story, but I trust Bernie [Moreno] so much as a good friend, and his family has such high values.” The West Virginia senator Shelley Moore Capito said: “I don’t know [Miller]. I haven’t read a whole lot about him, but if [Moreno] thinks he ought to resign, I’m supportive of that.” Lisa Murkowski, a Republican senator from Alaska, said: “The accusations are very serious, and if there is truth to them, I am one who says that our elected officials need to be held to high standards. “And certainly, when it comes to allegations of domestic abuse, child abuse, that’s not what we want in our lawmakers.” Three other senators, Rick Scott of Florida, West Virginia’s Jim Justice and Cynthia Lummis of Wyoming, also gave public backing to Moreno against Miller. “I don’t know enough about the allegations, but like Bernie said, it sounds like he thinks he needs psychological help,” said Scott. “I trust Bernie.” Miller – who married Emily Moreno at Trump’s club in Bedminster, New Jersey, in 2022 – has been accused of holding a gun to her head and scalding her with boiling water. Their toddler daughter, who was born in 2023, is also said to have suffered a broken collarbone due to his actions. Miller denies allegations of abuse and has filed a defamation case against his wife over the claims. The couple divorced in 2025. Axios reported that Trump called Miller on Monday amid concerns that the situation threatened Republican chances of holding the congressional seat in November’s midterms, when the party already faces an uphill challenge to keep its wafer-thin majority in the House of Representatives. But the president avoided taking sides when asked about the issue by reporters in the White House. “I know Max, he’s a good person. I mean, I always thought he was a very good person. And I’m going to let the families figure that out,” he said. Miller has resisted calls for him to withdraw from the race and told the Wall Street Journal that Trump “was supportive of me over the phone” on Monday’s call. “He said he had a poll with no detail, and I pushed back with our poll that has us winning by 9 with our message out there,” Miller told the newspaper. “He kept on reiterating it’s going to be tough, and it’s going to be a really hard one for you.” If Miller were to remove his name from the ballot before the close of business on Tuesday, a special Republican primary would be held to replace him. If he were to withdraw after that, the party would still need to replace him by 10 August, but would need to give two days’ notice beforehand to hold a meeting to choose a substitute candidate. • In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 0808 2000 247, or visit Women’s Aid. In Australia, the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found via www.befrienders.org.

fields.trailText: Max Miller says he has ‘nothing to hide’ amid domestic abuse allegations made against him by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, daughter of Republican Ohio senator Bernie Moreno
fields.bodyText: Thanks for following our live coverage of the second Trump administration. Stay tuned to our blog dedicated to the US midterm primary elections, where we’ll be watching the latest developments in Michigan, Kansas, Missouri, Virginia and Washington. Here are the highlights for today: The US Senate judiciary committee voted along party lines to advance Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general after he confirmed in writing that a planned $1.8bn slush fund for Donald Trump’s allies was dead. Experts say, however, that Trump could easily reverse the deal. More here. Max Miller, a US Republican representative from Ohio, is facing a rising groundswell of resignation calls from his own party over domestic abuse allegations after his ex-father-in-law, Bernie Moreno, a GOP senator, said he was unfit to serve in Congress. The House ethics committee announced it will launch an investigation into allegations that Miller “may have engaged in domestic violence and abuse or illegal drug use in violation of the code of official conduct or any other applicable standard of conduct” after the embattled Republican said he had “nothing to hide” and welcomed the investigation. More here. Jay Clayton has been sworn in as the US’s top spy after a contentious Senate confirmation hearing during which ⁠he refused to directly ⁠acknowledge that Donald Trump lost the 2020 presidential election. The oath of office was administered to Clayton on Tuesday by the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, in the Oval Office as the president looked on and applauded. More here. An attorney for the former Olympic canoeist who was charged with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool has said that “all options are on table” for legal recourse after prosecutors recently abandoned the case abruptly. David Hearn “has a number of potential remedies” after being prosecuted in connection with pool damage now attributed to faulty work by a contractor, attorney Steven Levin said in a statement. More here. A New York law banning US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents from wearing face coverings and requiring that they wear visible identification has been put on hold by a federal judge. But a state law prohibiting cooperation between local police departments and ICE has been allowed to stand. More here. Answering whether the release of a link containing private photographs of his daughter was reckless, Max Miller said that the incident “is being taken very much out of context.” “This is once again a very salacious headline,” Miller said. “I didn’t do this. My attorney took full responsibility. I believe that it’s awful. There was never any intent to do that.” Miller was also pressed by Jake Tapper on whether he believed the three women accusing him of violent behavior were all lying. “For no second am I going to sit here and continue to be debased by false and baseless allegations and be pushed out of a seat I have worked so hard to represent and done a terrific job for our community,” Miller said. “I’ve been a good legislator. All they’re trying to do is create rumor mills without evidence.” Asked whether he would consider dropping out of the race for the sake of his own mental health and his daughter’s well-being, Miller said he is “never going to give up.” “My daughter is going to grow up one day, and she’s going to see all of this, and she’s not going to see that her father caved to political and social media pressures,” Miller said. In an interview with CNN’s Jake Tapper, embattled Ohio representative Max Miller rejected claims from Senator Bernie Moreno (his former father-in-law) that Miller withheld his daughter’s favorite stuffed toy during a custody exchange. “I would agree that if that were true, that would be incredibly disturbing,” Miller told Tapper on Tuesday. “This is nothing more than an individual who’s being politically vindictive.” Moreno has called for Miller to withdraw from his re-election bid amid allegations of domestic abuse and seek professional help. On Tuesday, he described the experience as “truly the seventh level of hell” for his family. An instructor at the University of Maryland, Baltimore who only just received a “teacher of the year” award has been arrested by federal immigration agents under the command of the Trump administration. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officials detained Berhanu Kibret, an instructor at the university’s pharmacy school, at the Dallas-Fort Worth airport in Texas, according to multiple news reports. The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, confirmed Kibret’s arrest, citing an expired visa – but it stopped short of providing a location. In a statement, the University of Maryland said Kibret was arrested while returning from a meeting of the American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy, where he received a “teacher of the year” award. “Dr Kibret has a valid work authorization, so it is our hope that any issues surrounding his status will be quickly resolved and that he will be permitted to continue his work at the University of Maryland School of Pharmacy,” the institution added, according to CBS. The Associated Press is reporting that the Trump administration has revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to the United States in retaliation for Brazil’s denial of visas last month for two American diplomats who sought to visit the country ahead of upcoming elections as well as Brazil’s stalling on approving President Donald Trump’s nominee to be ambassador in Brazil. The state department said the decision was a reciprocal response to Brazil’s move and officials said the step had been delayed several times to give Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva room to back down, something he did not do. Officials said it could be quickly reversed if Brazil takes appropriate action and accepts Trump’s ambassadorial choice. Lula will face senator Flávio Bolsonaro , whose father once served as Brazil’s president and whose family has many ties with the Trump administration, in the 4 October polls. The administration has numerous issues with the leftist Lula and his policies and has also hosted the younger Bolsonaro, who is seeking to carry on his father, Jair’s, conservative governance. Joseph Gedeon reporting from Michigan: While outside a voting site in Dearborn, a confident Abdul El-Sayed not only believes he will win the primary, but has his sights set on Republican opponent Mike Rogers, predicting he “will beat [Rogers] by seven” in November. He called Rogers “generationally boring and generationally corrupt” adding that he “can’t decide what era of Republicanism he wants to be, so he carries the baggage of both.” “I’m hoping that that all of the senators who want to see a [Democratic] majority are going to team up, so we can all collectively dunk on Mike Rogers” he told reporters. The Trump administration is reportedly drafting a ban on US imports of new models of Chinese datacenter components, in the latest sign US authorities are scrambling to respond to the rapid development of AI technology in China. Four people familiar with the matter told Reuters that the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), which oversees the US ⁠telecommunications industry, is developing a measure to bar imports of new Chinese optical transceivers, which allow data to travel over fiber-optic cables at the speed of light within datacenters. Officials hope to publish the measure this year, according to Reuters. The FCC could still modify or shelve the restriction, Reuters reported. But the deliberations are the latest example the Trump administration is increasingly focused on limiting Chinese technological incursions into cutting-edge US industries. An attorney for the former Olympic canoeist who was charged with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool has said that “all options are on table” for legal recourse after prosecutors recently abandoned the case abruptly. David Hearn “has a number of potential remedies” after being prosecuted in connection with pool damage now attributed to faulty work by a contractor, attorney Steven Levin said in a statement. Levin added that those could include “civil suits, bar referrals for the prosecutors involved, request for sanctions and reimbursement of attorneys’ fees and expenses”, and requests for investigations by various government entities, including Congress. Hearn, 67, was arrested on 19 June and faced one felony count of property destruction – a charge that could have resulted in a 10-year prison sentence and a $1,000 fine – which he denied. Senate majority leader John Thune was asked about embattled House representative Max Miller, who is the ex-son-in-law of Republican senator Bernie Moreno. “It’s a family matter and, um, I don’t have any observations beyond that,” Thune said. When asked by a reporter about whether a member of Congress who is accused of domestic violence should continue to serve in their role, the Republican leader said: “It’s a House matter. It’s a family issue too.” The House ethics committee announced Tuesday it will launch an investigation into allegations that Max Miller “may have engaged in domestic violence and abuse or illegal drug use in violation of the code of official conduct or any other applicable standard of conduct”. The announcement comes hours after the embattled Republican from Ohio said he had “nothing to hide” and welcomed the investigation. Senator Bernie Moreno told reporters that the dispute between his daughter, Emily Moreno, and her ex-husband, Representative Max Miller, has been “truly the seventh level of hell.” “This has been a horrific experience for my entire family,” the Ohio senator said. Senator Moreno feared what could happen to his granddaughter, especially after Miller’s attorney accidentally released a private image of Miller’s child in documents shared by the congressman. “This has been brutal beyond comprehension, and if there’s any minimum standard for being an elected official, as I said, he fails to meet that minimum basic standard,” senator Moreno said. Senator Moreno said he had to handle the pickup of his two-year-old granddaughter over the weekend at a police station because he didn’t “want my daughter interacting with this man” and “I don’t know what this guy’s capable of.” US secretary of state Marco Rubio ⁠said there has been ⁠progress made in discussions with Iran ⁠and Oman on ‌getting ‌more ships through ‌the strait of Hormuz but no final agreement has been ‌reached. “There’s been progress made in those talks, but not finality yet. ⁠We’re hoping that will happen very shortly,” Rubio told reporters ‌at the State Department. As a reminder, my colleague Lucy Campbell is covering the latest developments in the Middle East. The live updates can be found here: Embattled GOP representative Max Miller is calling for a House investigation into himself amid domestic abuse allegations made against him by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, daughter of Republican Ohio senator Bernie Moreno. Miller is seeking a House ethics investigation into his own conduct as he faces growing calls to resign, including from his own party, in light of the accusations. In light of all the renewed interest in my family affairs I am going to file my own paperwork for an ethics investigation into myself to clear my name from these horrific attacks on myself and family,” the Ohio representative said in a post on social media. “I have absolutely nothing to hide. We will be providing the committee all necessary documents needed for a detail examination. The accusations continue to change, but my facts stay the same. I am looking forward to my colleagues reading everything for themselves.” Max Miller, a Republican representative from Ohio, is facing a rising groundswell of resignation calls from his own party over domestic abuse allegations after his ex-father-in-law, Bernie Moreno, a GOP senator, said he was unfit to serve in Congress. With a deadline looming for party leaders to choose a potential replacement, Miller, a former White House aide, also came under pressure from Donald Trump on Monday after the president reportedly called and told him “things aren’t looking good” for his re-election campaign against his Democratic opponent, Brian Poindexter. Pleas for Miller to step down intensified after Moreno – father of Miller’s former wife, Emily Moreno – broke his silence on Sunday after months of refraining from comment on allegations concerning the alleged abuse of his daughter. “If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them,” Moreno, an ally of Trump, posted. “He should not serve in the House of Representatives.” Moreno’s comments came after Miller posted a livestream video defending himself against the abuse accusations and saying his former wife had “significant mental-health challenges”. A series of public statements from Moreno’s fellow Republican senators indicate that their sympathies are with him. “[Miller] should resign. He should quit,” Roger Marshall, a senator from Kansas, told Politico. “I don’t know Mr Miller’s story, but I trust Bernie [Moreno] so much as a good friend, and his family has such high values.” The West Virginia senator Shelley Moore Capito said: “I don’t know [Miller]. I haven’t read a whole lot about him, but if [Moreno] thinks he ought to resign, I’m supportive of that.” The artificial intelligence company Open AI and the justice department reached a settlement in a case involving allegations that the company discriminated against US workers in favor of temporary visa holders during its Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) recruitment process. The justice department alleged that OpenAI omitted the job listings from its public career website that it sought to fill through the PERM process, which allows employers to hire foreign workers to work permanently in the US. DoJ also alleged the company required paper applications sent by mail and ran recruitment ads on late-night radio to keep US candidates from applying for these positions. OpenAI and its subsidiary Statsig Inc were accused of violating the Immigration and Nationality Act and will pay a combined $3,200,000. “It is illegal to discriminate against US workers by preferring temporary visa holders for jobs,” said assistant attorney general Harmeet K Dhillon of the DoJ’s Civil Rights Division. “This substantial settlement ensures that OpenAI redresses harm and changes its recruitment practices so that US workers receive a fair opportunity for highly sought-after technology positions.” Democrats have continued to express their concerns over Blanche’s agreement, warning that it doesn’t go far enough to prevent the Trump administration from claiming more immunity from tax audits or compensating Trump allies, including people who attacked the Capitol on 6 January 2021. Illinois senator Dick Durbin of Illinois, the top Democrat on the senate justice committee, said that the fund “can easily be revived with a new order from the Department of Justice 15 minutes after Mr. Blanche is confirmed as attorney general.” Meanwhile, on Monday, California senator Adam Schiff said on social media that the deal “doesn’t prevent payouts to violent insurrectionists in the future.” California’s Alex Padilla made similar remarks, saying that “nothing here stops DOJ from using taxpayer money to pay off January 6th insurrectionists. And it leaves the IRS shield protecting Trump and his family from past audits fully intact.” Senator John Cornyn said there is “no alternative but to take his word” regarding Todd Blanche’s decision to rescind a controversial “anti-weaponization” fund. “As to the idea it could be revived in the future, I think it’s highly unlikely that could happen without the cooperation of the department of justice,” Cornyn told reporters. “And I think Mr Blanche gave us the assurances that it was dead and would not be revived, and in this case we have no alternative but to take his word for that.” Blanche struck the deal with key Republican Senate holdouts, Cornyn and Thom Tillis, to secure support for his nomination. Under the agreement, Blanche formally rescinded the fund and clarified that the broad tax immunity the justice department granted to Trump only applied retroactively to the president, his sons, and businesses. The US Senate judiciary committee voted along party lines to advance Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general after he confirmed in writing that a planned $1.8bn slush fund for Donald Trump’s allies was dead. Experts say, however, that Trump could easily reverse the deal. His nomination will now proceed to the full Senate, where it will probably face intense skepticism from Democrats. Blanche, one of Donald Trump’s most trusted legal aides and formerly his personal defense lawyer, has faced questions over his suitability to lead the Department of Justice, which is supposed to operate independently of the White House. He signed an order scrapping the so-called Anti-Weaponization Fund – a roughly $1.8bn pool of money created in May as part of a settlement ending Trump’s lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service – in a bid to defuse a Republican rebellion over his nomination. Read the full story by Joseph Gedeon and Sam Levine: Commissioners for Tarrant County, which contains Fort Worth, Texas, will vote on Tuesday on a proposal to cut the number of polling locations by nearly half for the November election. The proposal has drawn sharp criticism from civil rights leaders and democracy activists. “Let’s call this what it is: voter suppression,” said NAACP president and CEO Derrick Johnson. “Cutting nearly half the places where people can cast a ballot doesn’t save democracy money, it costs voters their voice. Tarrant County is home to a significant number of Black and Latino voters and is a majority people-of-color county. There is no question that this plan strips away polling access on a scale that will hit Black and Brown voters hardest. That is not a coincidence. It’s an intentional assault on our ability to make our voices heard and we will push back with every tool available.” The commissioners court for Texas’ third-largest county has a Republican majority. Donald Trump won the county by a 52-47 margin in 2024, with more than 823,000 votes cast. The hearing began at 10am CST. The midterm election in Texas for the US Senate between Texas’ Republican attorney general Ken Paxton and the Democratic nominee, State Rep. James Talarico of Austin, is unusually tight for Texas politics. Talarico held a five-point lead in the most recent poll. The proposal reduces polling places in Tarrant County from 316 locations to 176 for this year’s election, and cuts the number of early voting polling places from 50 to 42. US Senator Dick Durbin of Illinois, ranking member of the senate judiciary committee, said he could not take acting US attorney general Todd Blanche at his word that the Trump administration would not reinstate a $1.8bn fund at issue in Blanche’s nomination. ”We have learned that simply his word is not enough for most of us, not even for some of my Republican friends,” Durbin said. “Even his word under oath is not credible enough.” Blanche, who negotiated the creation of the fund as part of a settlement with the IRS over a leak of the president’s tax returns, is Donald Trump’s former criminal defense attorney. Trump’s public commentary defending the settlement undermines Blanche’s assertion that the fund will no longer move forward, Durbin said, noting that Trump had not signed the order Blanche issued on Sunday that terminated the fund. ”Trump responded as we might have guessed, as he always does, by doubling down on his position and personally attacking our colleagues,” Durbin said. “To state the obvious: Mr Blanche’s statement on the slush fund and the IRS immunity agreement are not signed by the parties to the settlement agreement and are therefore unenforceable. The parties could still enforce the agreement, and the cop-beaters fund can easily be revived with a new order from the Department of Justice 15 minutes after Mr Blanche is confirmed as attorney general. Indeed, the president himself has loudly telegraphed that’s his plan.” US Senator John Cornyn of Texas said at the confirmation hearing for acting US attorney general Todd Blanche’s nomination that he is now satisfied by Blanche’s assurances that the $1.8bn “anti-weaponization” fund at issue is now dead. ”I’ve been very clear, as others have, that in other order to support Mr Blanche’s nomination, I needed specific assurances in writing about a release signed by the acting attorney general … that clarifies the scope of the parties to the IRS audit agreement and it permanently ends the [anti-weaponization] fund,” Cornyn said. “While this may sound like nitpicking to some, it’s critically important not only to me but to other members of the Senate. What Mr Blanche said under oath in his nomination hearing on these topics was important.” Cornyn and other Republicans have been holding up the nomination of Donald Trump’s former criminal defense attorney in order to obtain sufficient assurances that the fund proposed in a settlement to the president’s lawsuit stemming from the agency’s leak of his tax records would not go forward. Critics suggested that the “anti-weaponization” money would be used to reward January 6 rioters for their loyalty to the president. The Department of Justice issued a written order formally withdrawing the fund late on Sunday after negotiations between the Justice Department and outgoing Republican senators Cornyn and Thom Tillis of Kentucky. “They’ve been consistent about their assertion on behalf of the United States of America that the weaponization fund is dead,” Cornyn said. “Of course, I expect them to live up to that in any future litigation.” The White House has called an emergency summit of artificial intelligence business leaders on Tuesday to finalize details of a voluntary compliance system for safety breaches, following reports that two major AI tools had breached their digital containment and hacked external computer systems. Anthropic reported last week that models of its Claude tool successfully hacked into the infrastructure of three separate companies during red-teaming tests by exploiting weak passwords and unauthenticated endpoints. Anthropic said an external evaluation partner mistakenly granted the testing agent unfiltered internet access. That followed an announcement from ChatGPT developer OpenAI that an autonomous tool powered by its AI hacked the US startup Hugging Face and four other unnamed firms during an internal cybersecurity test. Both Anthropic and OpenAI have been invited to the summit, as have leaders from Google and Meta, according to Reuters. US Senator Darline Graham, sister of the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, said in a televised debate on Monday evening in Columbia, South Carolina that she would vote to end the filibuster in order to pass the Save America Act imposing additional federal rules on voting practices. While much of America’s political world is watching primary elections today in five states – Kansas, Michigan, Missouri, Virginia, and Washington – the special election for a successor to serve the remainder of Lindsey Graham’s term lands next Tuesday. South Carolina Governor Henry McMaster, a Republican, appointed Graham’s sister to serve until a new election is held. Darline Graham has the endorsement of Donald Trump, a point she made repeatedly at the debate. “I completely support the president’s agenda,” Graham said. “I’m 100 percent behind him. I’m honored to have his endorsement. I’ve been working with him on the Russia sanctions deal. I’ve co-sponsored the Save America Act.” Graham narrowly trails congressman Ralph Norman in the latest polling for the Republican nomination. Congressman Russell Fry, former South Carolina Governor Mark Sanford and businessman Mark Lynch are among 10 candidates in the contest. The death of immigration detainee Edwin Jovanny López Cornejo in custody on Saturday at Delaney Hall continues to reverberate among activists and political leaders critical of the ICE facility’s conditions. US representative Analilia Meija, a Democrat from northern New Jersey, said in a statement that her “gravest concerns about conditions for medically vulnerable people at Delaney Hall are now confirmed.” Meija, who won her seat in a special election earlier this year, said that “Edwin’s family has serious concerns about the medical treatment he received in detention, and I share those concerns. … This is not the first life we’ve lost inside that facility. New Jersey’s own health inspectors have been denied full access, including the medical unit, again and again. If there’s nothing to hide, there’s no reason to keep them out.” The death of Jean Wilson Brutus in December 2025 at the ICE facility in Newark, New Jersey began a round of protests which has led to a hunger strike by some detainees. Allegations of physical abuse by guards, medical neglect and spoiled food persist. Meija called for a full investigation by the Department of Homeland Security. “Abolishing and replacing ICE is the only way to correct this – a system that lets this happen again and again cannot be reformed,” she said. “It must be rebuilt around human dignity.” A far-right Republican candidate in Florida’s governor’s race has been accused of stiffing a high school debate champion over the better part of $11,000 in scholarship money she won from a company he founded. Student Briana Whatley landed the awards as regional and national champion of Incubate Debate, a league-style competition set up by the candidate, James Fishback, to encourage youth to engage in political discourse. A recording posted to Substack by Fishback in May 2024 shows Whatley, now a second-year history student at Florida State University, accepting a $10,000 check for besting seven other finalists in the 2024 Incubate Debate national championship, adding to two $500 area awards she previously won. According to Florida Politics, Whatley is suing Fishback for not delivering $8,000 of the money that a letter from the company promised would be paid to her in full on the day she graduated high school in May last year. The filing names Incubate Foundation Inc, the parent of Incubate Debate, and Fishback, 31, who is challenging front-running US congressman Byron Donalds and Jay Collins, the lieutenant governor of Florida, for the Republican nomination for state governor in November. The candidates face off in an 18 August primary. Donald Trump is making a rare visit to California and Nevada this week to try to draw contrasts with Democrats on the economy, border security and crime , seeking to shore up support for Republicans in November elections that will determine whether his party keeps control of Congress. The Republican president has struggled to connect with voters on the economy as elevated inflation and feelings of uncertainty have overshadowed the stock market gains he often talks about along with a low national unemployment rate, AP reports. Trump will visit the Los Angeles area on Tuesday to speak at a fundraising dinner for the Republican National Committee at a golf club his family owns in the suburb of Rancho Palos Verdes. On Wednesday, Trump will discuss the economy during an event at Red Rock casino in Las Vegas. New York cannot ban federal agents from wearing face coverings or require that they wear visible identification, a federal judge ruled on Monday. The ruling comes after a federal judge earlier this year blocked a similar law in California that was enacted after the Trump administration aggressively worked to increase immigration arrests, AP reported. For the Northern District of New York, US District Judge Mae D’Agostino wrote that while New York “appears to be well-intentioned in its pursuit of transparent policing,” that’s not what the court is deciding. “The issue now before the Court is about constitutionality—not transparency or preferable policy decisions,” she wrote. The federal government has shown a likelihood that the measures go against the supremacy clause of the US Constitution, which bars state governments from regulating federal law enforcement, D’Agostino wrote. The measures were included in a slate of law enforcement policies as part of the state budget bill that was signed into law by Democratic governor Kathy Hochul in May. Congressional seats, including one in Slotkin’s former district, are also in the mix in Michigan, with further tests of progressives’ rise. The progressive US senator Bernie Sanders has boosted El-Sayed and two progressive challengers in congressional races. In the Lansing-area seventh district, Sanders backed William Lawrence, a community organizer who co-founded the Sunrise Movement, over former US ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink and Matt Maasdam, a former US Navy Seal. Maasdam received Slotkin’s endorsement in the race for the purple district, currently held by Republican Tom Barrett. In the 13th district, Sanders boosted state representative Donavan McKinney, who is running against incumbent Democratic representative Shri Thanedar in the Detroit-area district. On the right, Republicans will figure out if they want to nominate John James, a US representative with Donald Trump’s endorsement, or businessman Perry Johnson to face Jocelyn Benson, the secretary of state and likely Democratic nominee for the governorship. James has led in polls, but late grassroots energy has given Johnson some momentum. Governor Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat, served for eight years and faced term limits preventing another run for the high office. Michigan is not the only state with primaries on Tuesday. In Missouri, voters will weigh whether to nominate former US representative Cori Bush, who is running to return to the chamber against Wesley Bell in a race punctuated by the war in Gaza and outside spending by pro-Israel groups. webTitle: Jay Clayton sworn in as US director of national intelligence

fields.headline: Jay Clayton sworn in as US director of national intelligence
fields.trailText: After a bumpy confirmation hearing, Clayton replaces acting director Bill Pulte to head US intelligence agencies
fields.bodyText: Jay Clayton has been sworn in as the US’s top spy after a contentious Senate confirmation hearing during which ⁠he refused to directly ⁠acknowledge that Donald Trump lost the 2020 presidential election. The oath of office was administered to Clayton on Tuesday by the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, in the Oval Office as the president looked on and applauded. He becomes the ninth director of national intelligence, replacing Tulsi Gabbard, who stepped down in June. Clayton, a former US attorney for the southern district of New York and chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), will oversee 18 US intelligence agencies. His appointment follows a turbulent two months in which the intelligence apparatus was temporarily led by Bill Pulte, the housing regulator whom Trump installed as acting director after Gabbard’s departure. Pulte’s appointment had unsettled some Republicans because of his lack of national security experience. During his brief tenure, however, he became involved in the administration’s increasingly prominent campaign to raise concerns about the integrity of US elections. Shortly before Clayton’s confirmation, Pulte released intelligence community documents from 2020 describing China’s capacity to interfere in US politics and vulnerabilities in the election system. The material was largely previously known but its release came as Trump has made “election security” a central political issue ahead of November’s midterm elections. Trump has continued to promote false claims that the 2020 election, which he lost to Joe Biden, was stolen. During Pulte’s tenure, he also released classified material that he said supported his arguments. Clayton’s own confirmation was overshadowed by the same issue. Democrats condemned his refusal to state that Biden had won the election, while Republicans ultimately confirmed him along party lines. The controversy has raised questions about how the intelligence community will operate under a president who has repeatedly accused federal agencies of being “weaponised” against him. In his first statement as director, Clayton sought to address those concerns, promising to protect the intelligence community from political interference. “The safety and security of the ‌American people will be ‌our North Star, and we will work to make sure the ‌American people have complete confidence in the [intelligence community] through proper oversight, transparency and accountability,” Clayton said in a press release from the office of the director of national intelligence. “This includes ensuring the vital work of our [intelligence community] is never weaponized for political motives,” he added, echoing language frequently used by Trump and his allies to describe their claims that previous administrations abused federal power to target the president. Clayton brings substantial experience in law enforcement and government to the job. As US attorney in Manhattan, he oversaw prosecutions involving terrorism, international drug trafficking and organised crime. Before that, he chaired the SEC from 2017 to 2020, where the administration says he oversaw more than 2,300 enforcement actions resulting in more than $10bn in penalties and disgorgement. He has also held senior positions in business and law, including at Apollo Global Management and Sullivan & Cromwell, and has taught at the University of Pennsylvania and Wharton. Republican senators have pointed to that record as evidence that Clayton is qualified to lead the intelligence community. John Thune, the Senate majority leader, has called him a “proven leader” whose record inspired confidence. Tom Cotton, the chair of the Senate intelligence committee, said Clayton had deep experience in national security threats. Other Republican supporters highlighted his previous bipartisan confirmation as SEC chair. Senator Katie Britt of Alabama added via X on Tuesday: “Congratulations to our Director of National Intelligence, Jay Clayton! I look forward to seeing him lead our intelligence community and keep our nation safe from threats.” Clayton now inherits an intelligence community that has already endured a succession of upheavals under Trump. Gabbard’s tenure was marked by clashes with congressional Democrats, who accused her of advancing the president’s political agenda and promoting debunked election claims. Pulte’s temporary appointment then raised fresh concerns about the politicisation of the intelligence agencies. Clayton said his aim was to create an intelligence organisation that was “streamlined, agile, team-oriented and mission-focused”. He added: “I look forward to making sure the men and women of the [intelligence community] have the resources they need to carry out our critical mission.” With just more than three months left before midterm elections that will decide which party controls Congress, Trump has escalated efforts ‌to make “election security” a central issue, despite established findings that voter fraud is rare.

webTitle: Washington state Democrat who flipped pro-Trump district faces tough primary

fields.headline: Washington state Democrat who flipped pro-Trump district faces tough primary
fields.trailText: Incumbent Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, a moderate who owns an auto repair shop, hopes to retain congressional seat
fields.bodyText: The two-term Democratic congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez is heading into one of the country’s most closely watched contests on Tuesday after national recognition for flipping a Republican seat in 2022. Representing Washington state’s third district, Gluesenkamp Perez finds herself squeezed between the Democrat and progressive Brent Hennrich and the Republican state senator John Braun on her right. There are six other candidates on a single crowded ballot and the top two finishers will advance to the November general election regardless of party. Democrats are favored to win the House of Representatives in November’s midterm election, but highly contested seats such as Gluesenkamp Perez’s will be crucial to securing a majority, and expanding the margin. Republican Jaime Herrera Beutler won Washington’s third district in 2010 and held it for six terms, until Gluesenkamp Perez narrowly beat Trump-endorsed Joe Kent in 2022. Trump has carried the district in all three of his presidential runs, most recently by about three points, and yet in 2024 Gluesenkamp Perez ran roughly seven points ahead of her party’s presidential nominee. Logging, mills, agriculture, shipping and manufacturing still shape daily life in much of the area and Gluesenkamp Perez’s success has stemmed from her appeal to moderates and rural voters. An auto repair shop owner, she won over many in south-west Washington, including Republicans who considered Kent too extreme. “We like her a lot,” said Laura Oltmann, 41, a resident and supporter who describes herself as a conservative. Kent did not embody conservatism, Oltmann said. But through Gluesenkamp Perez’s two terms, frustration has built among her own party, growing when Democrats saw her siding with Republicans on major legislation. Hennrich, who is challenging her in the primary, ran for the same seat in 2022 before standing down, but decided to run again. “I stepped out of this race to unify Democrats to help get Marie through, so we could get rid of our six-term incumbent, Jaime Herrera Beutler,” he said. “[Gluesenkamp Perez] has turned out to be just an absolute epic failure for Democrats.” Hennrich is not alone. Several local Democratic organizations inside the district have broken with her. “She ran as a Democrat and inspired a lot of people, and she won, and we thought she was going to be what we wanted her to be. But everybody’s disappointed,” said LaDonna Kirkpatrick, chair of the 18th legislative district Democrats, speaking in a personal capacity. Kirkpatrick traces that disappointment to Gluesenkamp Perez’s votes for the Save Act, Trump’s effort to overhaul elections, as well as for a bill restricting how public schools address gender identity, and federal funding tied to the war in Iran. She claims the congresswoman has also stopped talking to her own party’s local officers. Thea Zahn, the chair of the 20th legislative district, agreed. “What majority are you going for?” she said. “Are you going for a majority that believes in Democratic values, or a majority that will fail over and over again when it comes down to it, when you really need people to stand up and say this is what we believe in?” Asked if she would vote for the congresswoman if she is on the ballot in November, Zahn said: “I won’t vote for Marie. I will never vote for Marie Perez again.” The congresswoman’s defenders make a different argument: that the district’s partisan lean leaves her little room, and that the seat matters more than any single vote. “The reality is we live in a Republican district. It is Republican,” said Terri Niles, who chairs the 17th legislative district Democrats and spoke in a personal capacity. “I’ve knocked on tens of thousands of doors.” Niles argues that none of Gluesenkamp Perez’s contentious votes actually resulted in legislation passing, and that the calculation for Democrats is simpler than her critics allow. “The most important thing everybody should keep in mind is that flipping the House is our goal,” she said. “That should be the most important thing for every Democrat out there.” The Democratic infighting comes at a precarious moment. An Emerson College poll conducted in mid-July for the Northwest Progressive Institute found Gluesenkamp Perez and Republican Braun tied. Braun, the Republican leader in the Washington senate, has become one of the GOP’s top congressional recruits, earning Donald Trump’s endorsement in April and the backing of the National Republican Congressional Committee. “We could hand a truly 100% Maga candidate a congressional seat for life,” said Tim Probst, a local Democratic party leader. “Because once he gets in there, he’s not getting out.”

webTitle: Revealed: major oil firms make $93bn profits amid war and climate crisis

fields.headline: Revealed: major oil firms make $93bn profits amid war and climate crisis
fields.trailText: Iran conflict windfall over three months reignites calls for companies ‘cashing in on human misery’ to pay for environmental damage
fields.bodyText: Eight of the biggest oil companies amassed profits of more than $90bn (£67bn) in just three months as the Iran conflict sent energy prices soaring and the emissions-fuelled climate crisis caused deadly heatwaves. The windfall war profits have reignited calls for oil and gas supermajors such as Saudi Aramco and BP to pay for the environmental damage caused by “cashing in on human misery” and fund a rapid transition to renewable energy. Guardian analysis found that the eight listed oil producers made almost $93bn (£69bn) in the three months to the end of June – the first full financial quarter after the US-Israeli war on Iran triggered a surge in global oil prices to highs above $126 a barrel. The companies have used the biggest disruption of fossil fuel supplies in the market’s history to almost double their combined profits from just under $50bn in the same period last year, with campaigners warning that millions of households are left paying the price in higher bills and climate chaos. The data suggests the eight oil companies – Aramco, BP, Shell, Equinor, TotalEnergies, Eni, Chevron and ExxonMobil – made more than $700,000 of profit every minute over the spring quarter. While their market valuations were swelling by about $600bn to above $3tn, temperatures built towards a run of deadly heatwaves, all made more likely and more severe by burning fossil fuels. Carbon emissions from the world’s biggest fossil fuel firms were directly linked to fatal spells of hot weather for the first time by scientific analysis published last September. It found the emissions from any one of the 14 biggest companies were each enough to cause more than 50 heatwaves that would otherwise have been virtually impossible. The biggest oil profits in the spring quarter were raked in by Saudi Arabia’s state-owned oil company, Aramco, which reported a 34% increase in its quarterly net income to more than $33bn, even as its infrastructure was damaged by drone and missile strikes from Iranian and Houthi forces. Saudi Aramco’s fossil fuel production has made it responsible for more carbon emissions than any company in history, according to the database Carbon Majors, followed by Chevron and ExxonMobil and with Shell and BP in the top 10. Saudi Arabia has for decades led successful efforts to block and delay international climate action. On Tuesday, BP became one of the last big oil companies to publish its results for the April to June period, reporting quarterly profits of $5.73bn – the highest since the first year of Russia’s full-scale war on Ukraine and more than double the $2.5bn of the previous three months. Patrick Galey, the lead on fossil fuels at Global Witness, said: “BP’s sky-high profits are a scandalous reminder of who’s been cashing in on human misery this year. While wildfires threaten communities across the world, drought bites and energy costs spiral, ordinary families are paying the price for big oil’s prioritisation of shareholder wealth over a livable planet.” He added: “It’s time to make oil giants pay up to repair the climate breakdown they’re driving. Think how many fire and flood defences we could build, or how many solar panels we could install, if big oil paid their fair share in taxes.” Rosie Downes, the head of campaigns at Friends of the Earth, said: “While BP banks another round of enormous profits, millions of households are paying the price through sky-high energy bills and a climate crisis accelerating rapidly out of control.” BP’s new chief executive, Meg O’Neill, defended the company’s profits by saying it was “focused on the things we can do to try to help address the situation” such as reliably producing more of the oil products that were in short supply. The company has been cutting the amount it spends on green energy since it dropped its environmental ambitions in a “fundamental reset” early last year, reducing its annual energy transition budget from $5bn to $1.5bn-$2bn. In recent years BP has spun off its UK offshore windfarms into a joint venture and sold its US onshore wind business, and on Tuesday it announced it would sell its $4bn US biogas business, which captures methane from landfill sites and is the largest renewable gas producer in the US. It is in advanced talks to sell its solar power business, Lightsource, to a consortium backed by Kuwait’s sovereign wealth fund, according to the Financial Times. On Friday, BP put its North Sea oil and gas business up for sale after more than 60 years operating it, reigniting calls for the UK government to rule out the development of two controversial North Sea fields in the ageing basin. Shell last week reported its second highest quarterly profits ever as its net income jumped to $9.84bn, despite producing less gas from its Qatar gas plant due to billions of dollars’ worth of damage caused by the war. Equinor’s profits climbed to $3.2bn in the same period, up from $1.8bn in the spring quarter last year. In the US, the profits reported by Chevron and ExxonMobil provoked criticism from Donald Trump. The US president accused the pair of “making too much money” from his war on Iran and warned that they would be made to return profits to the public, as he nears the November midterm elections with flagging approval ratings. Chevron reported net income of $12.2bn for the second quarter, a more than fivefold increase on the same period last year. ExxonMobil reported a profit of $14.5bn, double what it made in the same period a year ago and its highest quarterly profit since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Galey said: “You know big oil is taking us for a ride when one of their biggest allies, Donald Trump, is telling them to rein their profiteering in.” The impacts this summer include Europe’s worst ever heatwave, another categorised by scientists as “impossible” without human-caused global heating. About 20,000 people are estimated to have died due to the extreme temperatures, including close to 3,000 in the UK in May and June alone. South Korea and Japan have also experienced record-breaking heat of up to 42.5C, with the Korean weather agency instructing people to “immediately stop all outdoor activities”, while the climate crisis pushed up temperatures across much of Africa in July. Global heating makes every heatwave more intense and more likely, and rising global temperatures kill one person a minute around the world, a report in the Lancet estimated in October. The UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, said: “Around the world, climate-driven disasters are reaching nightmare proportions. What needs to be done is clear: leave coal, oil and gas behind faster, scale up renewables, and protect people where the impacts are already hitting hardest.” Europe’s succession of heatwaves has sucked soils dry and led to extreme drought, damaging food supplies from maize to sunflowers to salad. At least 9m tonnes of grain are expected to be lost, with the UK, for example, facing its worst harvest on record. The arid conditions have also enabled huge wildfires in France, Spain, Portugal and Greece, causing billions of euros of damage. The blazes send toxic air pollution soaring and in the US and Canada the fires from 15-23 July are estimated to have caused about 4,000 deaths within a week of exposure. The climate crisis is making fire weather worse and about 1.5 million people a year have their lives shortened by wildfire smoke. In south Asia, the climate crisis is supercharging extreme rainfall – air that is 1C warmer holds 7% more water. More than 40cm of rain fell in 24 hours in Chattogram in Bangladesh in early July, for example, leading to flash flooding. Floods and landslides have taken lives and livelihoods in Pakistan and India. There have also been dozens of fatalities in north-west China, where many thousands of people have been evacuated due to heavy storms. The eight oil companies were contacted for comment. The Guardian’s climate forum 2026: on Tuesday 20 October, join Damian Carrington and our panel of experts – including Prof Andy Haines, Katie White MP, Asad Rehman, Shruti Suresh, Gareth Thomas and Amy Fairman – for a hopeful and solutions-focused evening. Book tickets here or at guardian.live.

webTitle: Trump accuses oil companies of ‘making too much money’ from his war on Iran

fields.headline: Trump accuses oil companies of ‘making too much money’ from his war on Iran
fields.trailText: US president hits out at ExxonMobil and Chevron, saying they should ‘give some of that back to the public’
fields.bodyText: Donald Trump has criticised oil companies for “making too much money” from the global energy market disruption caused by his war on Iran. Brent crude had been trading at about $70 (£52) a barrel before the first US-Israeli strikes at the end of February, but by the end of April it had soared as high as $126 and is now trading at about $85 a barrel. The US president took aim at the windfall profits revealed last week by ExxonMobil and Chevron, and said the companies would “give some of that back to the public”. “They’re making too much money based on a shortage,” he told reporters at the White House on Monday evening. “I don’t like it.” Trump was speaking just hours before BP reported its profits had doubled in the last quarter, to $5.7bn. The US oil companies made profits totalling more than $26bn for the three months to the end of June by taking advantage of the energy market disruption triggered by the US-Israeli war on Iran. Chevron reported its highest ever quarterly profit of $12.2bn, a fivefold increase on the same period last year. ExxonMobil reported a profit of $14.5bn in the second quarter, double what it made in the same period a year ago and its highest quarterly profit since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. “Chevron: too much money. ExxonMobil: too much money,” Trump said. “They’re going to give some of that back to the public and they better cut the retail price, the consumer price.” Asked about Trump’s comments, the BP chief executive, Meg O’Neill, told CNBC that she understood the pressures on households. “The reality is, we produce a global commodity, and the product we sell hangs off that global commodity price,” she added. Climate campaigners have also attacked big oil’s bumper quarterly earnings, condemning them as “obscene”. Clémence Dubois, a campaigns director at 350.org, an international environmental group, said: “Chevron and Exxon are profiteering from a model of distraction, leaving ordinary people to pay the price with higher bills and devastating impacts such as these fires. These profits feel almost criminal.” Trump criticised oil company profits weeks after warning energy retailers to cut their prices as he nears the November midterm elections with flagging approval ratings. He also ordered the US justice department to investigate potential price gouging in the retail energy sector. “Gasoline Retailers must get their Prices down, IMMEDIATELY,” he wrote on his Truth Social platform in late June. “If Retailers don’t do this, big problems lie ahead!” The president told journalists that the fall in oil and gas prices during the administration’s June peace talks with Iran should have caused petrol prices to fall to $2.25 a gallon. “Oil prices have come down so much and we are not seeing anything at the pump by comparison the way they should be,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. US gasoline prices currently average $4.11 a gallon, according to data from the AAA motoring group. The Trump administration has repeatedly said it has no plans to introduce an export ban on oil or petroleum products, but some analysts say this could be revisited if prices at the pump continue to rise.

webTitle: Trump declines to call for Max Miller’s resignation amid abuse allegations – as it happened

fields.headline: Trump declines to call for Max Miller’s resignation amid abuse allegations – as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: And that brings our live coverage of the second Trump administration to a close for the day. We’ll be back on Tuesday. Here are the latest developments: Donald Trump declined to call for Rep Max Miller’s resignation following allegations of domestic abuse from his ex-wife, Emily Moreno. Trump said he has always known Miller as “a good person” and called the situation “a very sad thing.” In an 89-4 vote, the Senate voted to take up a measure that would temporarily keep the government funded and help avoid a shutdown in the fall. The measure, known as a continuing resolution, would maintain government funding at current levels through 11 December, with some adjustments for specific programs. The Senate is slated to debate the funding bill and move it closer to a final vote. Two Republican senators who threatened to block Todd Blanche’s bid to permanently become US attorney general announced they will advance his nomination after he said in writing that a planned $1.8bn slush fund for Donald Trump’s allies was dead. Legal experts and Democrats said what Blanche announced Sunday was far from ironclad and left room for Trump to resurrect the fund. More here. A coalition of 25 US states sued the Trump administration over new tariffs pegged at 10% to 12.5% on goods from 60 trading partners, calling them a pretext for replacing import taxes struck down by the supreme court in February. The states are asking the US Court of International Trade to halt the tariffs, declare them unlawful and order refunds of duties that have already been paid. More here. Trump accused US attorney Jeanine Pirro of having “folded like an umbrella” amid reports that he was considering removing her from her post. Trump criticized Pirro on Monday after she dropped vandalism charges against a former Olympian accused of damaging the recently renovated Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool. More here. A far-right Republican candidate in Florida’s governor’s race has been accused of stiffing a high school debate champion over the better part of $11,000 in scholarship money she won from a company he founded. Student Briana Whatley landed the awards as regional and national champion of Incubate Debate, a league-style competition set up by the candidate, James Fishback, to encourage youth to engage in political discourse. A recording posted to Substack by Fishback in May 2024 shows Whatley, now a second-year history student at Florida State University, accepting a $10,000 check for besting seven other finalists in the 2024 Incubate Debate national championship, adding to two $500 area awards she previously won. According to Florida Politics, Whatley is suing Fishback for not delivering $8,000 of the money that a letter from the company promised would be paid to her in full on the day she graduated high school in May last year. Construction crews building a border wall in New Mexico were ordered to stop drilling new wells after ranchers said that pumping groundwater to produce concrete could threaten their livestock amid a severe drought. At a public meeting in July, ranchers said they were noticing unmonitored tapping of border aquifers that threatened the water for those nearby. “Whatever they do on that well affects everybody in this basin,” one rancher said in the meeting, adding that, from his conversation with border patrol, he believed that “they really don’t even understand what an aquifer is.” A spokesperson for Customs and Border Protection told the AP on Monday that border wall contractors in New Mexico have been instructed to stop drilling new wells. “CBP is committed to working collaboratively with local landowners to ensure that construction activities do not adversely impact their water needs,” said CBP in a statement. Previously, CBP, which oversees the border wall construction, has said water is needed to produce concrete, build roads, construct barriers and control dust at construction sites. New Mexico’s Office of the State Engineer told NPR last month that it counted at least six wells under development along the border, and that none had the necessary permits required by state law. The US state department is planning to close five foreign missions, reducing its diplomatic footprint in the Caribbean, Asia, Africa and North America, Reuters reports. According to a notice obtained by the outlet, the department said it plans to close its posts in St. George’s, Grenada; ⁠Nagoya, Japan; Medan, Indonesia; Douala, Cameroon; and Winnipeg, Canada. The notice, sent to several congressional committees last week, follows similar moves at the beginning of Trump’s second term, when the administration announced plans to close a dozen foreign missions to align with his “America first” agenda. In an 89-4 vote, the Senate voted to take up a measure that would temporarily keep the government funded and help avoid a shutdown in the fall. The measure, known as a continuing resolution, would maintain government funding at current levels through 11 December, with some adjustments for specific programs. The Senate is slated to debate the funding bill and move it closer to a final vote. The US House of Representatives ethics committee on Monday recommended that Chuck Edwards, a Republican congressman, face censure after determining he “fostered a hostile work environment and engaged in sexual harassment” by giving gifts and lavishing attention on two young female staffers. The bipartisan panel began investigating the second-term North Carolina congressman earlier this year, after receiving complaints about his conduct. In their report, they determined Edwards broke House rules by singling out the two unidentified aides for special treatment that made them uncomfortable and harmed relations with other employees. While the investigation uncovered no evidence that Edwards engaged in sexual activity with the staffers or suggested it, his behavior violated provisions in the House code of conduct that prohibit sexual harassment and unwanted advances. The congressman “acknowledged at least some of the behavior at issue could be viewed as inappropriate”, but “has not acknowledged or taken responsibility for the harm he caused”, the committee wrote in its report. A compromise between Todd Blanche and two Republican senators that potentially cleared the way for Blanche’s confirmation as attorney general is weak, Democrats and several experts said, as it makes promises Donald Trump can easily reverse. Blanche, the acting attorney general, posted two documents on Sunday evening showing he was withdrawing an 18 May order allowing for the creation of a $1.8bn weaponization fund and clarifying that broad tax immunity the justice department granted to Trump only applied retroactively to the president, his sons, and businesses. The agreement stemmed from a deal worked out with senators John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, two Republicans who had threatened to block Blanche’s nomination. Cornyn and Tillis said on Monday they would support Blanche when his vote comes up for the Senate judiciary committee Tuesday. “We are pleased that the Department of Justice has issued a formal order terminating the anti-weaponization fund,” Cornyn and Tillis said. “Additionally, the department has acknowledged in a binding written order that the audit settlement is limited to the plaintiffs and the scope does not extend beyond the defendants in the lawsuit, the IRS and the treasury, addressing concerns that multiple of our Republican colleagues share.” But legal experts and Democrats said what Blanche announced Sunday was far from ironclad and left room for Trump to resurrect the fund. “These assurances are not worth the paper they’re written on,” Brandon DeBot, policy director at the Tax Law Center at NYU, said in a statement. “They don’t pull back on the ongoing attempts to give the president, his family, and his affiliates unauthorized immunity from tax audits. They don’t do anything new to stop the president from trying to bring back the fund, as he threatened to this weekend. It’s abundantly clear we need congressional action.” A group of 25 states sued the Trump administration over a round of tariffs that went into effect last month, arguing that the US president exceeded his legal authority to tax imports after the US supreme court struck down his previous set of global tariffs. “President Trump is so intent on raising the cost of living for Americans that he is willing to break law after law after law to do so,” said California attorney general Rob Bonta in a statement. “Tariffs are taxes, and the American people cannot and should not shoulder the extra costs that come from the President’s failed and illegal economic policy — no matter how much the President wants them to.” The lawsuit challenges tariffs of 10% to 12.5% imposed on dozens of countries, including the UK, Mexico, Canada, Australia, India, China and the 27 countries that make up the European Union, which took effect on 24 July. The Trump administration said it imposed the tariffs in an effort to stop exports of goods produced with forced labor. But states argue the latest measures are an unlawful attempt to replace tariffs the courts have repeatedly rejected. In February, the US supreme court declared many of Trump’s tariffs illegal in a 6-3 ruling, deciding that a 1977 law designed to address national emergencies did not provide the legal justification for most of the Trump administration’s tariffs.
